options_template.text: Consumption falls during the recession and rises when the price drops.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Normal-Good Response Applied to Inferior Good): For an inferior good, lower income during a recession INCREASES demand rather than reducing it.

options_template.text: Consumption rises during the recession (lower income raises demand for an inferior good) AND rises during the 30% price discount (the positive substitution effect outweighs the smaller negative income effect).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Lower income directly boosts demand for an inferior good, while a price cut raises quantity demanded because for any ordinary (non-Giffen) inferior good, |SE| > |IE|.

options_template.text: Consumption rises during the recession, but falls during the 30% price discount because the income effect always dominates for inferior goods.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (All-Inferior-Are-Giffen Error): The income effect dominates only in the rare Giffen case; the prompt specifies an ordinary (non-Giffen) inferior good.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Empirical Rarity of Giffen Goods
questions.title: Why Giffen Goods Are Virtually Absent in High-Income Economies
questions.prompt_template: Why do economists observe virtually no Giffen goods in modern high-income economies, even though many everyday products (such as generic store-brand staples) are inferior goods?

hints.text: Think about the two conditions required for a Giffen good in Section 11.3: inferiority AND budget share.
Look at the Slutsky income-effect term -X * (∂X / ∂I): what happens to its magnitude when spending on X is a tiny share of income?

options_template.text: Because consumers in high-income economies do not experience diminishing marginal utility.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (DMU Denial): Diminishing marginal utility applies across all income levels and is not what prevents Giffen behavior.

options_template.text: Because the substitution effect is zero in modern economies due to brand loyalty.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-SE Reversal): If SE were zero, an inferior good would be MORE likely—not less likely—to exhibit Giffen behavior.

options_template.text: Because modern governments prohibit prices of inferior goods from ever rising.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Institutional Myth): Prices of inferior goods fluctuate freely in market economies; the absence of Giffen behavior stems from household budget shares.

options_template.text: Because any single inferior staple represents too small a share of a typical household's total budget for its income effect to overpower the negative substitution effect.
options_template.feedback: Correct. In the Slutsky equation, the income effect scales with quantity/budget share (-X * ∂X/∂I); when a staple accounts for only a tiny fraction of household spending, the income effect is far too weak to overturn the negative substitution effect.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Corner Solutions and the Equimarginal Rule in Grocery Shopping
questions.title: Why a Rational Shopper Might Buy Zero $12 Organic Berries
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a shopper genuinely enjoys $12 organic berries more per carton than $3 bunches of bananas, yet buys several bunches of bananas and zero cartons of organic berries. How does the equimarginal framework explain this rational corner solution?

hints.text: Compare the ratio MU / P for the first carton of $12 berries against the last bunch of $3 bananas.
How many times higher must MU_berries be than MU_bananas for a dollar spent on berries to match a dollar spent on bananas?

options_template.text: Even for the very first carton, MU_berries / $12 is still strictly less than MU_bananas / $3 at the shopper's chosen banana quantity, so every dollar yields more satisfaction on bananas.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Berries must deliver more than four times the marginal utility of bananas to justify four times the price; if MU_berries / $12 < MU_bananas / $3 even at Q_berries = 1, buying zero berries maximizes utility.

options_template.text: The shopper is acting irrationally because rational utility maximization always requires buying positive quantities of every liked good.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Interior-Only Myth): Utility maximization allows corner solutions whenever one good's MU / P remains below another's even at the first unit.

options_template.text: Organic berries must have negative marginal utility for this shopper.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Negative-MU Assumption): A good can have high positive MU and still not be purchased if its price is so high that MU / P is beaten by alternatives.

options_template.text: The shopper's indifference curves must be upward sloping because they bought zero berries.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Preference-Violation Error): Standard downward-sloping convex indifference curves easily yield corner solutions when the budget line is steeper or flatter than every curve along an axis.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Tax Incidence on the Budget Line: Broad Sales Tax vs. Income Tax
questions.title: Comparing a Uniform Ad Valorem Tax on All Goods to a Proportional Income Tax
questions.prompt_template: In the two-good model with no saving or borrowing, suppose the government imposes a uniform 20% sales tax on BOTH Good X and Good Y (raising prices to 1.20Px and 1.20Py). How does this tax alter the consumer's budget line compared with a single-good tax on Good X alone?

hints.text: Write the post-tax budget equation 1.20Px * X + 1.20Py * Y = I and divide both sides by 1.20.
Check what happens to the slope -(1.20Px) / (1.20Py) and to both intercepts.

options_template.text: It pivots the budget line inward along the X-axis only, distorting relative prices just like a single-good tax.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Single-Good Pivot Confusion): Because BOTH prices rise by the exact same 20% factor, the ratio (1.20Px) / (1.20Py) = Px / Py does not change.

options_template.text: It shifts the budget line inward in parallel without distorting the relative price Px / Py, acting just like an equivalent reduction in nominal income.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Dividing 1.20Px * X + 1.20Py * Y = I by 1.20 yields Px * X + Py * Y = I / 1.20, preserving the exact slope -Px / Py while shifting the budget line inward in parallel.

options_template.text: It leaves the budget line unchanged because taxing both goods cancels out the purchasing-power loss.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cancellation Error): While the 1.20 factor cancels in the slope, it reduces both intercepts to I / (1.20Px) and I / (1.20Py), shrinking real purchasing power.

options_template.text: It rotates the budget line outward because tax revenue increases total market prices.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Direction-of-Tax Error): Higher after-tax prices shrink the consumer's affordable budget set inward, not outward.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Nonlinear Pricing: Flat Discount vs. Buy-One-Get-One-Half-Off
questions.title: How Quantity Discounts Reshape Marginal Incentives Along a Budget Constraint
questions.prompt_template: A campus bookstore considers two promotions on $20 notebooks (Good X): (1) a flat 25% discount ($15 per notebook on all units), or (2) 'Buy 1 at $20, get the 2nd at 50% off ($10).' Both promotions charge $30 total for 2 notebooks. How do their budget-line slopes differ for a student deciding whether to buy 1 notebook versus 2 notebooks?

hints.text: Compare the marginal dollar cost of the 1st notebook and the 2nd notebook under each pricing structure.
Recall that a higher marginal price produces a steeper budget-line segment, while a lower marginal price produces a flatter segment.

options_template.text: Both promotions create the exact same straight budget line because 2 notebooks cost $30 under either offer.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Average-vs-Marginal Price Confusion): Although the average price of 2 notebooks is $15 under both offers, the marginal price of the 1st unit ($20 vs. $15) and the 2nd unit ($10 vs. $15) differ sharply.

options_template.text: The flat 25% discount creates a steeper slope after the first notebook than the BOGO 50%-off promotion, making a 2nd notebook relatively more expensive at the margin under the BOGO offer.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Slope-Magnitude Reversal): A $10 marginal price on the 2nd notebook under BOGO is LOWER (flatter slope) than the $15 marginal price under the flat discount.

options_template.text: The flat 25% discount lowers the marginal price on the very first notebook ($15), whereas the BOGO offer keeps the budget line steeper on the first unit ($20) and then kinks flatter on the second unit ($10), strongly incentivizing 1-notebook buyers to add a 2nd.
options_template.feedback: Correct. BOGO 50%-off creates a kinked budget constraint: a higher marginal relative price on unit 1 ($20) followed by a sharply lower marginal relative price on unit 2 ($10), creating a stronger marginal pull from 1 to 2 units.

options_template.text: Neither promotion changes the slope of the budget line because the student's income I did not change.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Income-Only Slope Myth): The slope of the budget line is governed by marginal relative prices (-Px / Py), which both discounts directly alter.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Ordinal Utility and Policy Limits on Interpersonal Comparisons
questions.title: Why Ordinal Utility Prevents Purely Scientific Interpersonal Utility Sums
questions.prompt_template: During a public debate over redistributing $100 from a high-income household to a low-income household, a commentator claims: 'Because of diminishing marginal utility, we can mathematically prove that total societal utils increase by an exact number.' Why does modern ordinal utility theory caution against claiming an exact mathematical proof of total societal utils?

hints.text: Recall the distinction between ordinal rankings and cardinal measurements introduced in Section 11.2.
Ask whether multiplying Person A's utility numbers by 10 changes Person A's choices—and what it would do to a naive sum U_A + U_B.

options_template.text: Because diminishing marginal utility applies only to food, never to money income.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Scope-Restriction Error): While diminishing MU can apply to income for an individual, the deeper problem is comparing subjective utility scales across two different people.

options_template.text: Because low-income households always have lower marginal utility of income than high-income households.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Unsupported Cardinal Claim): Claiming one person's MU is lower than another's makes the exact same interpersonal cardinal assumption that ordinal utility rejects.

options_template.text: Because transferring $100 always lowers the recipient's total utility due to the income effect.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Non-Satiation Violation): Receiving $100 expands the recipient's budget set and raises their utility under non-satiation.

options_template.text: Because utility is ordinal—utility numbers only rank bundles within one person's preferences and cannot be measured on a shared cardinal thermometer or summed objectively across different people without normative value judgments.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Ordinal utility cannot objectively weigh one person's lost satisfaction against another person's gained satisfaction; redistribution debates inherently combine economic trade-offs with explicit normative equity judgments.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Diminishing Marginal Utility at an All-You-Can-Eat Dining Hall
questions.title: Optimal Consumption When Marginal Price Equals Zero
questions.prompt_template: Compare a student paying $4 per plate at a campus café versus paying a fixed $12 entry fee at an all-you-can-eat dining hall where every additional plate has a marginal price of $0. What does marginal-utility theory predict about consumption inside the all-you-can-eat hall?

hints.text: Once you have already paid the $12 entry fee, what is the marginal cost of taking one more plate of food?
Apply the rule: keep consuming additional units as long as marginal benefit (MU) exceeds marginal cost ($0).

options_template.text: Once inside, the $12 fee is sunk and the marginal price of an extra plate is $0, so the student keeps eating until marginal utility approaches zero (where total utility peaks), consuming more than under $4-per-plate pricing.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Under per-plate pricing, the student stops where MU / $4 equals the marginal utility per dollar of other goods (MU > 0); at a $0 marginal price, any plate with MU > 0 adds net satisfaction, pushing consumption to MU = 0.

options_template.text: The student will eat until marginal utility becomes strongly negative so that they 'get their money's worth' out of the $12 entry fee.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sunk-Cost Fallacy): Eating past MU = 0 into MU < 0 reduces total utility; a rational consumer ignores the sunk $12 fee and stops where MU reaches 0.

options_template.text: The student will eat the exact same number of plates under both pricing plans because preferences did not change.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ignoring Relative Prices): Consumption depends on both preferences and marginal price; dropping marginal price from $4 to $0 triggers a strong movement along the consumer's demand curve.

options_template.text: The student will eat fewer plates at the all-you-can-eat hall because the $12 upfront fee reduces their income more than $4 per plate.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ignoring Zero Marginal Price): Even with the $12 entry fee, facing a $0 marginal price eliminates the opportunity cost of additional plates, driving higher consumption per visit.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: In-Kind Vouchers vs. Cash Raises: Inframarginal vs. Extramarginal Consumers
questions.title: Predicting Who Loses Utility Under a Dedicated Transit Voucher vs. Cash
questions.prompt_template: An employer offers commuters a dedicated $100/month transit-only voucher (cannot be resold or spent on other goods) instead of an unrestricted $100/month cash raise. Consider Commuter A, who would spend $160/month on transit with a $100 cash raise, and Commuter B, who would spend only $40/month on transit with a $100 cash raise. How does the voucher affect each commuter's utility compared to the $100 cash raise?

hints.text: Ask for each commuter: if they received $100 in cash instead, would they already spend at least $100 on transit?
If a commuter already spends more than $100 on transit, a $100 transit voucher frees up $100 of their own cash to spend anywhere.

options_template.text: Both Commuter A and Commuter B are strictly worse off under the transit voucher than under the $100 cash raise.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Overgeneralizing In-Kind Distortion): Because Commuter A already wants to spend $160 > $100 on transit, the $100 voucher simply frees up $100 of their own cash for other goods, leaving Commuter A just as well off as cash.

options_template.text: Commuter A achieves the exact same utility as under the $100 cash raise (the voucher frees up $100 of their own transit budget), whereas Commuter B is constrained at the kink and strictly worse off than under cash.
options_template.feedback: Correct. For inframarginal Commuter A ($160 > $100), the $100 voucher is equivalent to cash; for extramarginal Commuter B ($40 < $100), the voucher forces $100 of transit consumption when B would prefer $60 of other goods, lowering utility.

options_template.text: Commuter B achieves higher utility under the voucher than under cash because the voucher forces healthy transit habits.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Restricting Choice Raises Utility): Narrowing a consumer's affordable set (preventing them from spending $60 of the $100 on non-transit goods) can never raise their utility above unrestricted cash.

options_template.text: Commuter A is strictly worse off under the voucher while Commuter B is unaffected.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inframarginal-Extramarginal Reversal): It is Commuter B—whose desired transit spending ($40) is below the $100 voucher—who is constrained and made strictly worse off.
